newsitem.title: USA: U.S. forex options market braces for EMU.
newsitem.headline: U.S. forex options market braces for EMU.

text.p: The creation of a single European currency will result in sweeping changes in the U.S. foreign exchange options market and, despite its tenuous nature, is already sending tremors through the industry, experts say.

As Europe continues to make halting progress toward European Monetary Union, U.S. exchanges and over-the-counter dealers are beginning to discuss the impact of the "Euro" on a market that trades well over $20 billion worth of contracts a day.

Among the greatest changes expected are a substantial drop in trade of options on European currencies, and a reallocation of some of that business to the emerging markets and to European interest-rate options, brokers say.

The Chicago Mercantile Exchange, which trades options on currency futures, recently appointed a committee to study the "major opportunities and significant challenges" posed by EMU, according to an exchange memo sent to members and staff.
Similarly, the Philadelphia Stock Exchange, which trades options on currencies, is conducting internal studies on the issue and plans to release a White Paper within a few weeks.

However, the greatest effect of EMU will be felt by the OTC markets. Eighty-seven percent of foreign exchange options traded in the U.S in the first quarter of 1996 changed hands through the OTC market, according to the Comptroller of the Currency Administrator of National Banks, in Washington, D.C.
According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, that accounts for $19.9 billion of trade a day. Of that, roughly half is done in contracts which include European currencies.

"Certainly there's going to be an impact on everybody's business," said one OTC dealer with a major investment house. "Putting those all into one currency has got to decrease business by 30 percent, I think, 30 percent or 40 percent."
Dealers said they expect to see such losses mitigated by several factors, the most obvious being gains in currency options activity in Latin America, Asia, and Eastern Europe.
Options trade in emerging markets is already growing. However, it will receive an addititional boost as some of the options business lost through monetary union shifts to other markets, they said.

"A trend, obviously, is that you'll see a growing amount of business from the non-first tier currencies," said Oliver Jefferson, vice president, Societe Generale. "But that won't replace the reduction in business for those currencies that disappear."
Jefferson cited options activity on the Dutch guilder as an example of what may happen to other currency options as monetary union approaches

Because the guilder tracks the German mark very closely, the relationship between the two exchange rates is very stable -- in options terms there is little "volatility" -- which means there is virtually no need to use guilder/mark options to hedge against sudden swings in the cross rate.
"What happens to an options market, if there's no volatility, is it disappears because there's no purpose in having options," Jefferson said.

Conversely, options on highly volatile currencies -- such as those of emerging markets -- provide traders with a greater oppportunity to make money through wide price swings, and therefore tend to be more liquid.

This is significant because an amalgamation of several European currencies is likely to be more volatile than the German mark, the most stable European currency. For that reason, Euro options could be more liquid than mark options -- which are already very liquid -- a fact that could help mitigate some of the loss of business, he said.
Greg Kaldor, vice president of currency option sales at Bank of America, said several other factors could reduce the loss of business caused by monetary union.

As speculation about convergence rates for the currencies builds prior to monetary union, there could be a spike in options business as customers attempt to hedge their positions against that uncertainty, he said. This effect will be particularly dramatic if there are repeated delays, which will increase the degree of uncertainty.

Also, while the need to hedge currency risk will disappear with EMU, there could be greater volatility in the interest rate markets of the European economies. This could lead to greater demand for interest rate derivatives, Kaldor said.
"We expect to see more interest in options on bond spreads between the Euro countries," he said.
Another dealer said he expects to see an increase in some exotic currency options to fill the void created by the loss of cross-rate business.

He cited one complicated range binary option, which dealers sardonically refer to as a SCUD (secondary currency unhedgeable derivative). The option is based on one currency but becomes valuable or worthless depending on the movement of a second.
Such instruments are currently very illiquid but could become more common when some European "plain vanilla options" are phased out, he said.
However, Jefferson disagreed, maintaining that highly speculative options are unlikely ever to become widely used.

"I don't think the development of the products has anything to do with the introduction of a currency union," he said. "There's always new products ... The question is how many of these ideas are really practical or how many are just bets that you could make by going to a casino?"
